sermons.life_context: Luther was professor of biblical exegesis at Wittenberg and had preached at the town church since 1514. His 1517 theses on indulgences had drawn him into open controversy. He refused to recant before Cardinal Cajetan at Augsburg in October 1518, and in July 1519 he debated Johann Eck at Leipzig, where he questioned papal primacy.

Luther was professor of biblical exegesis and a preacher at Wittenberg. The sermon appeared in the second half of 1519, the year of his Leipzig debate with Johann Eck (July), where he questioned papal primacy. According to J. J. Schindel, Duke George of Saxony complained about it on 27 December 1519 to Elector Frederick and two bishops, chiefly because it called for communion in both kinds.

Luther had been hiding at the Wartburg near Eisenach since May 1521 as 'Junker Jörg', under Elector Frederick's protection, and wrote this model sermon there that year. Earlier in 1521 he had been excommunicated, had refused to recant at the Diet of Worms and had been placed under the imperial ban. He signed the dedication of this part of the postil 'in the desert'.

Luther had just returned to Wittenberg, arriving on 6 March 1522 after leaving his Wartburg hiding place on 1 March against the Elector's instruction. At the Wartburg he had translated the New Testament into German. While he was away, Karlstadt, Gabriel Zwilling and others had pushed through rapid changes amid disturbances in which images were torn from the parish church.

The winter part of the Church Postil, which contains this model sermon, appeared in 1525. Luther was then in Wittenberg, where he preached, lectured and advised on church reform. In that year's Peasants' War he first urged peace, then in a May tract called on rulers to put down the revolt by force, and on 13 June he married the former nun Katharina von Bora.

This model sermon was printed in the Church Postil's winter part in 1525. Luther was living in Wittenberg, preaching, lecturing and advising on church reform. That year, during the Peasants' War, he wrote a May tract calling on rulers to crush the revolt, and in June he married the former nun Katharina von Bora, with whom he set up home in the Black Cloister.

The winter part of the Church Postil, which includes this model sermon, appeared in 1525. Luther was in Wittenberg, preaching, lecturing and advising on church reform. In the Peasants' War that year he first urged peace, then called on rulers to put down the revolt, which drew lasting criticism, and in June he married the former nun Katharina von Bora.

When this model sermon appeared in the Church Postil's winter part in 1525, Luther was in Wittenberg, where he preached, lectured and advised on church reform. That year brought the Peasants' War, in which he wrote a May tract urging rulers to crush the rebels. On 13 June he married Katharina von Bora, and they made their home in Wittenberg's former Augustinian friary.

Luther was travelling with Elector John's party toward the Diet of Augsburg and had reached Coburg, where he stayed from April to October 1530. German Wikipedia, citing Brecht, says he moved up to the Veste Coburg only on the night of 23–24 April. The Weimar editors say he chose the cross as his theme because his followers were accused of teaching nothing but faith.

Luther was living at the Veste Coburg, where he stayed from April to October 1530 during the Diet of Augsburg, while Melanchthon was in Augsburg. A letter of 5 June had brought him news of his father's death on 29 May. On 5 July he wrote to Melanchthon that he was meditating an exhortation for schools.

Luther was back in Wittenberg after spending April to October 1530 at Coburg Castle during the Diet of Augsburg. While at Coburg, in June, he had learned of his father's death. From 9 November 1530, while Johannes Bugenhagen was away from Wittenberg, he took on regular weekday preaching on Matthew and John.

In January 1546 Luther travelled to Eisleben, his birthplace, to help settle inheritance and legal disputes among the counts of Mansfeld, and he preached at Halle and Eisleben on this last journey. He had lectured at Wittenberg until 17 November 1545 and was troubled more and more by kidney stones and other illnesses. He died in Eisleben on 18 February 1546, days after this sermon.
